title: Peter by the fire (Mark 14:66–72)
hook: a servant girl, a denial, the rooster twice, and Peter breaks down weeping

segments.voice: Yesterday, a trial at night and two words, I am. Your line was silence can be strong. Did you take a breath before defending yourself? Day two hundred twenty-four, the end of the week.

While Jesus stands before the council upstairs, Mark cuts back to the courtyard below. Peter is there, the one who said earlier that same night, even if everyone else falls away, not I. When the others fled, he followed, at a distance, right into the high priest's courtyard. That took courage. He's sitting with the servants by a fire, warming himself. And one of the high priest's servant girls walks past, stops, and looks at him. Really looks. You were with the Nazarene, she says. You were with Jesus. It's not a soldier. It's not a judge. It's a young woman with a job to do, and one sentence.
screen: `MEANWHILE, THE COURTYARD.` → `A FIRE, AND PETER.` → `YOU WERE WITH JESUS.`

segments.voice: I don't know what you're talking about, Peter says, and he moves out to the gateway. And a rooster crows. The girl sees him again and tells the people standing around: this is one of them. He denies it again. A little later the bystanders try: surely you're one of them, you're a Galilean; they can hear it in his accent. And Peter, in the King James Bible, "began to curse and to swear, saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak." Three denials, each one louder. Right then the rooster crows a second time, just as Jesus said it would: before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. In Mark, the rooster crows twice. And then Mark gives us one short, plain sentence: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." Here's a curious thing. The Greek word behind when he thought thereon is rare and hard to pin down. Translators have guessed: he broke down, he threw himself down, he covered his head. Nobody is sure. But the verb for wept is clear, and its tense suggests he kept on weeping. Notice the timing. Upstairs, Jesus is telling the truth and it will cost him his life. Downstairs, Peter is lying to save his. Mark sets them side by side. And tradition links Mark's gospel to Peter's own preaching; if so, Peter told this story on himself. He doesn't hide the failure. The weeping is where he starts again. This week we've gone from perfume, to the upper room, to a garden where he prayed abba, to a kiss, a trial, and now a fire.
screen: `THE SERVANT GIRL.` · `THREE DENIALS, LOUDER EACH TIME.` · `THE ROOSTER CROWS TWICE.` · `WHEN HE THOUGHT THEREON, HE WEPT.` · then, large: `I KNOW NOT THIS MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let yourself grieve a failure. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you let someone down, or let yourself down. Not the worst thing you've ever done; something real but manageable. Instead of explaining it away, just let yourself feel sorry for it. Sadness isn't the end of the story. For Peter, it was the turning point. If tears come, let them. If you pray, you can bring that failure to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Peter, warming himself by the fire while three denials slip out, and a rooster crows twice. Then he breaks down weeping.
Your line: he wept. Today, if an old failure comes to mind, don't rush past it. Give it a moment of honest sorrow, and then let it be the start of something. Day two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Christians read Peter's denial in Holy Week, and a rooster became a common symbol of Peter and of repentance, carved on church towers and pictured in art of his weeping.

fork.reveal: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." Mark keeps Peter's failure in, and Christians often see it as the start of his turning back.

original.note: Greek: he wept, in a tense that can mean he kept on weeping. the last word of Mark 14.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter was a coward.
what it means: he followed as far as the courtyard, he fails, and he weeps.
what a scholar hears: the verb before he wept is a puzzle, epibalon, which translators render broke down, threw himself down or covered his head.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Fixed a narrative error: Peter's boast (Mark 14:29–31) was earlier the same night, not "a few nights ago". Cut "the only one of the twelve who followed this far", "only Mark has the rooster crowing twice" and "one of the saddest sentences in the Bible" as unsourced superlatives; "many early Christians linked" now "tradition links". Myth, fork and trapdoor aligned.
The link between Mark's gospel and Peter's preaching is tradition (Papias, via Eusebius); phrased as 'many early Christians linked' and 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Mark 14:72 epibalon: renderings vary; confirm the three examples given.
The imperfect eklaien read as continuous weeping ('can mean he kept on weeping'); confirm.
Rooster as symbol of Peter on church towers: common in art; confirm phrasing.
